# Warp Drive Spacetime — A Guided Tour *Space is allowed to stretch. Relativity forbids overtaking a light ray in your own neighbourhood; it says nothing about how much distance a neighbourhood contains. This page follows that loophole all the way to the end, and shows exactly what it costs and what it breaks.* --- ## 1. The one idea Fix a direction $x$, a ship trajectory $x_s(t)$ with speed $v_s = \dot x_s$, and a **shape function** $f$ that equals $1$ at the ship and falls to $0$ far away, depending only on the distance $$r_s = \sqrt{(x - x_s(t))^2 + y^2 + z^2}$$ from the ship. Declare the geometry of spacetime to be $$ds^2 = -\,dt^2 + \bigl(dx - v_s f(r_s)\,dt\bigr)^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 .$$ Far away $f = 0$ and this is ordinary flat spacetime. At the ship $f = 1$, and the worldline $x = x_s(t)$ has $dx = v_s\,dt$, so the bracket vanishes and $ds^2 = -dt^2$ exactly. The ship drifts freely, its clock ticking off ordinary seconds — and its coordinate velocity $v_s$ may be $10$, or $1000$, or anything at all. Everything about the *pointwise* causal structure depends on one number, the **local warp factor** $w = v_s f(r_s)$, through the quadratic form $$Q_w(u) = -(u^t)^2 + (u^x - w\,u^t)^2 + (u^y)^2 + (u^z)^2 .$$
Click to reveal: why this really is a spacetime, and not just notation $Q_w$ is the Minkowski form composed with the shear $S_w : (t,x,y,z) \mapsto (t,\,x - wt,\,y,\,z)$, a linear map of determinant $1$. In matrix form $S_w^{\mathsf T}\eta\,S_w = g(w)$ with $\eta = \mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Two consequences hold for **every** shape function, speed and event: - $\det g(w) = -1$: the metric never degenerates, so its Einstein tensor exists everywhere and $T_{\mu\nu} = G_{\mu\nu}/8\pi$ *defines* a matter distribution sourcing it exactly. - By Sylvester's law of inertia the signature is $(-,+,+,+)$ everywhere. So "is the warp metric a solution of Einstein's equations?" is, strictly, trivial: it is, by construction. All the physics is in the **sign and size** of that stress-energy — which is what the rest of this page is about. A short primer on the [3+1 (ADM) formulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADM_formalism) used throughout: the lapse here is $\alpha = 1$, the spatial slices are flat, and the shift is $\beta^i = (-v_s f, 0, 0)$.
--- ## 2. Play with the bubble Before any theorems, get your hands on the object. Slide the warp speed, the bubble radius and the wall thickness, and watch three things at once: where the negative energy lives, where space is expanding and contracting, and what the bill comes to. {{interactive_demo:0}} Three experiments worth doing right now: 1. **Thin the wall.** Drag $\Delta$ toward zero. The energy diverges like $1/\Delta$. That is not a flaw of this particular wall — it is a theorem, proved in §6 below. 2. **Double the speed.** The cost multiplies by exactly **four**, not two. The popular estimate "energy $\sim$ mass $\times$ speed" is off by a whole power of the speed. 3. **Set the speed to zero.** The exotic matter vanishes completely. Negative energy is the price of *motion*, not of the geometry. --- ## 3. Faster than light without going faster than light The observers naturally attached to this geometry — the ones who see the slices $t = \text{const}$ as their own instantaneous space — have four-velocity $n = (1, w, 0, 0)$, and $Q_w(n) = -1$: they are ordinary unit-timelike, freely falling observers, drifting with the local flow of space. The ship, sitting where $f = 1$ so $w = v_s$, has the *same* four-velocity. Its speed relative to its neighbours is exactly zero. > **Theorem (Effective superluminal travel without local superluminal travel).** For every warp speed $v_s$, the ship's four-velocity $(1, v_s, 0, 0)$ is unit timelike, its coordinate velocity is exactly $v_s$ — unbounded — and its velocity relative to the local freely-falling observers is exactly zero. Moreover every timelike direction $u$ at an event with warp factor $w$ satisfies > $$\left| \frac{u^x}{u^t} - w \right| < 1 .$$ Compare with the ambient flat region, where $w = 0$: there the four-vector $(1, v, 0, 0)$ with $v > 1$ has $Q_0 = v^2 - 1 > 0$ — spacelike, forbidden. **The same coordinate motion is illegal outside the bubble and perfectly ordinary inside it**, because the bubble carries its light cones with it.
Click to reveal: the two-line proof of the local speed bound First, coordinate time is a global time function: if $u^t = 0$ then $Q_w(u) = (u^x)^2 + (u^y)^2 + (u^z)^2 \ge 0$, with equality only for $u = 0$. So a nonzero causal vector has $u^t \ne 0$. (Equivalently $g^{tt} = -1 < 0$. This single fact will forbid closed causal curves in §7.) Now let $u$ be timelike. Then $(u^x - w u^t)^2 + (u^y)^2 + (u^z)^2 < (u^t)^2$, hence $(u^x - wu^t)^2 < (u^t)^2$; dividing by $(u^t)^2 > 0$ gives $\bigl(u^x/u^t - w\bigr)^2 < 1$. $\blacksquare$
**A price paid immediately.** In the region where $f < 1 - 1/v_s$ — which necessarily exists once $v_s > 1$, since $f \to 0$ at infinity — every future-directed causal curve falls strictly behind the bubble centre. Signals from inside cannot reach the front wall: the bubble has a horizon, and the crew cannot steer. --- ## 4. Where the motion comes from: expansion astern, contraction ahead The freely falling observers form a congruence whose volume expansion rate is $$\theta = v_s\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = v_s\, f'(r_s)\,\frac{x - x_s}{r_s} .$$ A shape function decreases outward, so $f' < 0$, and the picture reads off at once. > **Theorem.** With $v_s > 0$ and $f' < 0$: $\theta > 0$ everywhere behind the ship, $\theta < 0$ everywhere ahead, $\theta = 0$ exactly on the transverse plane through the ship, and $\theta(x_s + s) = -\theta(x_s - s)$ — perfectly odd. Space is *created* astern and *destroyed* ahead in exactly balanced amounts. The ship is not pushed; it is carried, the way a surfer is carried by a wave made of nothing but the rearrangement of water already there. {{visualization:0}} --- ## 5. The bill is negative — unconditionally Because the slices are flat and the lapse is unity, the Hamiltonian constraint of general relativity — the component of Einstein's equations fixing the energy density these observers measure — collapses to a purely algebraic identity, $$16\pi \rho = \theta^2 - \theta_{ij}\theta^{ij},$$ and for the warp field the right-hand side is a perfect **negative** square. > **Theorem (Unconditional exotic matter).** The energy density measured by the freely falling observers is > $$\rho = -\frac{v_s^2}{32\pi}\Bigl( (\partial_y f)^2 + (\partial_z f)^2 \Bigr) \;\le\; 0$$ > for **every** shape function and **every** warp speed. In spherically symmetric form, > $$\rho = -\frac{1}{8\pi}\,\frac{v_s^2\,(y^2+z^2)}{4\,r_s^2}\,\bigl(f'(r_s)\bigr)^{2}.$$ > It vanishes exactly on the axis of motion and wherever the wall is locally constant, and is strictly negative everywhere else. Two things matter here. First, this is not a design flaw: the density is *minus a sum of squares*, so no shape function can make it nonnegative anywhere. The [weak energy condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_condition) is violated unconditionally. Second, the factor $y^2 + z^2$ vanishes on the axis: the exotic matter is a **torus** encircling the direction of travel, with empty space directly fore and aft.
Click to reveal: the algebraic identity that forces the negative sign The expansion tensor of the Eulerian congruence, written through the gradient $g_k = \partial_k f$, is $$\theta_{ij} = v_s\begin{pmatrix} g_x & g_y/2 & g_z/2 \\ g_y/2 & 0 & 0 \\ g_z/2 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \theta = v_s g_x .$$ Summing squares gives $\theta_{ij}\theta^{ij} = v_s^2 g_x^2 + \frac{v_s^2}{2}(g_y^2 + g_z^2)$, so $$\theta^2 - \theta_{ij}\theta^{ij} = -\frac{v_s^2}{2}\bigl(g_y^2 + g_z^2\bigr).$$ The trace-squared cancels **exactly**, leaving minus the squared *transverse* gradient. Divide by $16\pi$ and you have the theorem.
Click to reveal: the other half of Einstein's equations — the exotic matter must flow The momentum constraint fixes the energy flux. Writing $H_{ij} = \partial_i\partial_j f$ for the Hessian of the shape function, $$8\pi j^x = -\tfrac{v_s}{2}\bigl(\partial_y^2 f + \partial_z^2 f\bigr), \qquad 8\pi j^y = \tfrac{v_s}{2}\partial_x\partial_y f, \qquad 8\pi j^z = \tfrac{v_s}{2}\partial_x\partial_z f .$$ The source is momentum-free only if the shape function is transversally harmonic *and* has no mixed second derivatives — which no genuine bubble wall satisfies. So the exotic matter cannot be static dust in the bubble frame: **it must flow**. Note the scaling degrees: $\rho$ is quadratic in $v_s$, while $j^i$ is *linear*. That mismatch is the whole story of the next section.
{{algorithm:3}} --- ## 6. How much, exactly — and why no clever engineer can make it cheap Integrating the density over a slice (the angular average $\langle (y^2+z^2)/r^2\rangle = 2/3$ collapses everything to one dimension) gives $$E = -\frac{v_s^2}{12}\int_0^\infty f'(r)^2\, r^2\, dr .$$ For the simplest design — a bubble of radius $R$ whose wall is a linear ramp of thickness $\Delta$, so $f' = -1/\Delta$ across the wall — the integral is elementary: > **Theorem (Exact thin-wall energy).** For $\Delta < 2R$, > $$E(v_s, R, \Delta) \;=\; -\frac{v_s^2}{12}\left( \frac{R^2}{\Delta} + \frac{\Delta}{12} \right).$$ {{algorithm:0}} ### The linear conjecture dies > **Theorem (Quadratic, not linear).** $E(\lambda v_s) = \lambda^2 E(v_s)$ for every shape function. Hence for any fixed geometry there is **no** constant $C$ — in particular no multiple of the ship mass — with $E = C\,v_s$ for all speeds; and for every putative coefficient $M > 0$ there is a threshold speed beyond which $|E| > M v_s$. The reason is structural: the Hamiltonian constraint is *exactly quadratic* in the extrinsic curvature, and the extrinsic curvature is *exactly linear* in the warp speed. Two times one is two. (The naive $M v_s c$ guess is the correct scaling — for the *momentum*, not the energy.) ### The floor no profile can beat The linear ramp is crude. Could a subtler wall be dramatically cheaper? The question is well-posed: a shape function must fall from $1$ at the inner edge of a shell $a \le r \le b$ to $0$ at the outer edge, so its derivative $g = f'$ obeys $\int_a^b g\,dr = -1$; minimise $\int_a^b g^2 r^2\,dr$. > **Theorem (Sharp geometric floor).** For every admissible profile supported in the shell $0 < a \le r \le b$, > $$\int_a^b g(r)^2 r^2\,dr \;\ge\; \frac{ab}{b-a},$$ > attained exactly by $g^*(r) = -\dfrac{ab}{(b-a)r^2}$, i.e. by the shape function $f^*(r) = \dfrac{a}{r}\cdot\dfrac{b-r}{b-a}$.
Click to reveal: the completed-square proof (three lines) Put $\lambda = ab/(b-a)$. For every $r \in [a,b]$, $$g(r)^2r^2 + 2\lambda\,g(r) + \frac{\lambda^2}{r^2} = \left(g(r)\,r + \frac{\lambda}{r}\right)^{\!2} \ \ge\ 0 .$$ Integrate over $[a,b]$, and use the normalisation $\int g = -1$ together with the elementary identity $\int_a^b r^{-2}\,dr = \frac1a - \frac1b = 1/\lambda$: $$0 \le I[g] - 2\lambda + \lambda = I[g] - \lambda . \qquad \blacksquare$$ Equality forces $g(r)r = -\lambda/r$ pointwise, i.e. $g = g^*$. This is [Cauchy–Schwarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Schwarz_inequality) in its completed-square disguise, and the extremiser is exactly the Euler–Lagrange solution of the constrained problem.
For a shell of thickness $\Delta$ centred at $R$ the floor equals $R^2/\Delta - \Delta/4$ — the *same* $1/\Delta$ divergence as the crude ramp, which in fact misses the optimum by only $v_s^2\Delta/36$. **The thin-wall catastrophe is a theorem, not an artefact.** {{algorithm:1}} Don't take the bound on faith — attack it numerically. The next demo throws thousands of random admissible wall profiles at the floor and confirms that none ever beats it, then perturbs the optimal profile and watches the excess grow exactly quadratically, precisely as the completed square predicts. {{demo:1}} {{visualization:1}} --- ## 7. Does the warp drive build a time machine? A dichotomy Superluminal travel and causality are famously in tension: "faster than light" in one frame is "backwards in time" in another. Here the answer splits cleanly in two, and both halves are theorems. ### One bubble is harmless > **Theorem (Chronology protection for a single bubble).** No Alcubierre spacetime contains a closed causal curve — for any shape function, any warp speed, any trajectory.
Click to reveal: Rolle's theorem does all the work Because $g^{tt} = -1$, coordinate time $t$ is a global time function: along any causal curve its derivative $u^t$ can never vanish (§3). Suppose a closed causal curve existed, $\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)$. Then $t(s) = \gamma^0(s)$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, differentiable on $(0,1)$, and $t(0) = t(1)$, so [Rolle's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolle%27s_theorem) hands us a point where $\dot t = 0$. Contradiction. $\blacksquare$ Geometrically: the spacetime is foliated by flat Cauchy slices. It is globally hyperbolic and chronologically well behaved.
### Two bubbles are not The catch is that a warp corridor must be **built**, at rest in *some* inertial frame — and different builders may choose different frames. A traveller takes a corridor at rest in the background frame $S$, of effective speed $V > 1$, for a duration $T$: from the origin to the event $(T, VT)$. The separation is $$-T^2 + (VT)^2 = T^2(V^2 - 1) > 0 : \quad \textbf{spacelike}.$$ No ordinary causal curve joins departure to arrival — yet inside the corridor the same leg is a unit-timelike worldline. That contrast is what the warp bubble buys, and it is also what makes it dangerous. > **Theorem (Two corridors close a loop).** For every effective warp speed $V > 1$ and every duration $T > 0$, take the boost velocity > $$\beta = \frac{2V}{V^2+1} \in (0,1), \qquad \text{which satisfies } \beta V > 1 .$$ > Then in the boosted frame the arrival event sits at time exactly $-T$ and position exactly $VT$, so a second corridor of the same effective speed $V$, built at rest in that frame and pointed backwards, returns the traveller after the strictly positive duration $s = T$ **to the exact event they departed from**. Drive the construction yourself — change the speed, change the duration, and watch the loop close to machine zero every time: {{interactive_demo:1}} {{visualization:2}} {{algorithm:2}} **The moral.** Closed timelike curves are *not* a property of the warp metric. They are a property of the **existence of two independently oriented warp corridors**. One warp drive is a curiosity; two, aimed by parties who disagree about what "at rest" means, are a telephone to yesterday — the geometric incarnation of the [tachyonic antitelephone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tachyonic_antitelephone). The inconsistent combination is not warp travel alone, but *superluminal transport plus Lorentz invariance*. Any consistent theory permitting warp corridors must break the arbitrariness of the second corridor's rest frame. --- ## 8. Anti-gravity, quantified There is a deeper way to see *why* the negative energy is necessary. Gravity focuses: a bundle of freely falling observers with convergence $\theta_0 < 0$ is driven to a caustic in finite time, provided matter obeys an energy condition. The governing [Raychaudhuri inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raychaudhuri_equation), degraded by a violation of size $c \ge 0$, reads $d\theta/d\lambda \le -\theta^2/m + c$. The warp bubble supplies exactly such a defect, of size $c_{\text{warp}} = -16\pi\rho = \frac{v_s^2}{2}\bigl((\partial_y f)^2 + (\partial_z f)^2\bigr) \ge 0$, positive precisely on the toroidal exotic region. > **Theorem (Critical convergence).** A congruence entering the wall with $\theta_0^2 > m\,c_{\text{warp}}$ still focuses, within affine parameter $m|\theta_0|/(\theta_0^2 - m\,c_{\text{warp}})$. At the critical value $\theta_0^2 = m\,c_{\text{warp}}$ the guarantee fails: an eternal, never-focusing solution exists. And $c_{\text{warp}}$ is quadratic in $v_s$, so doubling the warp speed quadruples the focusing the drive can defeat. The exotic matter is of *precisely* the strength needed to defeat gravitational focusing. Negative energy is not a bookkeeping artefact; it is the anti-gravity the geometry must hire to hold its light cones tilted. --- ## 9. Run everything One script, no dependencies, reproducing every quantitative claim on this page: the unimodular-shear identity and $\det g = -1$; the unit-timelike ship at unbounded coordinate speed; the expansion dipole and its exact oddness; the nonpositive, axis-vanishing energy density; the exact thin-wall energy checked against direct quadrature; the fourfold cost of doubling the speed; the unbeaten geometric floor and the $v_s^2\Delta/36$ gap; and the two-corridor loop closing to machine precision. {{demo:0}} --- ## 10. What we now know - The warp geometry is a perfectly good Lorentzian spacetime, everywhere nondegenerate, sourcing a definite matter distribution. - It genuinely delivers unbounded coordinate speed with zero local speed, by expanding space astern and contracting it ahead in exactly balanced amounts. - Its matter content has negative energy density — unconditionally — shaped into a torus around the axis of travel, and it necessarily flows. - The energy scales as the **square** of the warp speed, refuting the popular linear guess, and diverges like $1/\Delta$ as the wall thins, with a sharp geometric floor $ab/(b-a)$ that no engineering can beat. - One bubble cannot make a time machine; two bubbles in relative motion demonstrably can, by an explicit two-leg construction with boost velocity $2V/(V^2+1)$. Whether nature permits macroscopic negative energy remains open. But if it does, the mathematics is now unambiguous about what one would be buying, what it would cost, and what one would be risking. The warp drive is not impossible because it is fast. It is *dangerous* because it is fast — and expensive in a way that grows faster than anyone hoped.
